speakers: Alan Dunne (host, sitting in for Niels, allocator/researcher)
Yoav Git (guest co-host, quant CTA researcher, Cambridge)
summary: Systematic Investor ep. 362 (Aug 2025): Yoav Git discusses a futures-curve (spread) trend paper, COT-based evidence that trend is not at capacity, the Bank of England FX derivatives paper, and his blog on how CTAs fit with long-term capital-market-assumption allocators (Vanguard 30/70). Main conclusions: trade spreads only after dislocations create risk, speculator positioning shows no trend crowding, and long-horizon allocators are mean-reverting so systematic strategies complement them.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: it has been a very difficult uh period for trend in fixed income
claims.claim: Trend following in fixed income has been difficult in 2025 because US yields oscillate indeterminately, while Japan shows a persistent climb and other markets show opposite drifts.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they've started a long climb back in 2022 from zero now sitting at an all-time high last night
claims.claim: Japan's 10-year yield rose steadily from zero in 2022 to an all-time high in August 2025, a persistent trend benefiting trend followers.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the idea that monetary policy will um kind of have to adapt to the fiscal stance you know when debt levels get so great
claims.claim: Fiscal dominance (monetary policy bending to fiscal needs at high debt) is becoming a market theme alongside rising Japanese yields.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: recommending that investors increase their allocations to hedge funds by 5%
claims.claim: BlackRock recommended raising hedge fund allocations by 5%, reflecting a more volatile macro environment, though CTA allocators remain hesitant after poor H1 returns.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: I think there is a general malaise in the CTA industry. Investors are waiting to see what's happening.
claims.claim: Investors hold off allocating to CTAs after six months of poor performance regardless of manager, even though the case for CTAs persists.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: alltime performance of CTAs, the reasons why they should invest in CTAs is that actually hasn't gone away at all
claims.claim: The long-run reasons to hold CTAs are unchanged by a weak period.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: year to date the trend index down 8 and a half% and the sock CTA index down just under 7%
claims.claim: As of late August 2025 the SG Trend index was down about 8.5% YTD and the SG CTA index nearly 7% down, with fixed income trends in Japan and Europe helping and FX/equities rangy.
claims.indicator: SG Trend index, SG CTA index

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: it will be a mistake to look at at you know, one month performance, two months per even six month performance
claims.claim: Judge trend following over long periods, not one to six months; it is painful like going down the stairs and up the elevator.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you're buying that that uh beautiful zero correlation to the um to the rest of the rest of your portfolio while you have a dynamic adjustment to market conditions
claims.claim: Trend following offers zero correlation to the rest of a portfolio plus dynamic adaptation, a fundamental reason to hold it.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you can buy corn for delivery at different months and the different months may behave differently right
claims.claim: A commodity is not one object: contracts for different delivery months (old crop vs new crop) differ by supply, demand, regulation, so curve points can be traded separately.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if I look at the difference between two deliveries two contracts Suddenly sometimes you get a dislocation uh and they behave differently
claims.claim: Policy shocks such as copper tariffs create dislocations between adjacent contract spreads because one contract falls before and one after the tariff.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the front of the curve is generally the one which is more volatile in the commodity business world and it is the one which is more affected by macronuse flow
claims.claim: The front of the commodity curve is more volatile and driven by macro news, while long-dated prices follow long-term supply and demand.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: when other players come onto the markets they tend to congregate where the the liquidity is and the front of the curve is where the liquidity is
claims.claim: New participants crowd into the liquid front contract, increasing volume there.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: spreads exhibit strong breakouts and reversals and I like I like the what they say about breakouts because the um when spreads actually break do break out it's actually quite violent
claims.claim: Calendar spreads show strong breakouts and reversals, and breakouts are violent, so a breakout rule fits spread trading.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they allocate to each of the individual markets and that allocation is relatively static over time
claims.claim: Traditional CTAs hold roughly constant risk allocations per outright market, but this cannot be done for spreads.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if you try to make this spread provide you with that risk you will have to leverage your position to such an extent that when a dislocation does happen you will be out of business
claims.claim: Spread volatility is itself volatile, so targeting constant risk needs huge leverage and wipes you out in a dislocation (left-skewed).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you have to wait until actually a dislocation happens you can't get into the trade first
claims.claim: Only start trading a spread after a dislocation lifts its volatility to a minimum level, then size it dynamically.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: being able to allocate meaningful risk to risk factors that um rise and they are transient by nature is something which I think is quite important
claims.claim: Allocating risk to transient risk factors (such as spreads) adds diversification because they are uncorrelated to the rest of the portfolio.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: a lot of managers trade spreads more from I suppose for the spread to revert to more mean reversion
claims.claim: Most managers trade spreads for mean reversion/carry, not breakout trend.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the play for the convergence of these two things is is normally the carriage rate and it's a kind of a nice and slow process.
claims.claim: Spread convergence follows cost of carry (interest, storage, convenience yield) and is slow, while dislocations arise when contracts are not substitutable.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if the two objects are funible then you will expect them to converge.
claims.claim: If two contracts are fungible they converge; a supply shock to one crop year breaks that and produces divergence.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: Okay. So then what you have is you have a real reason for that divergence between those spreads and that will create a a trend.
claims.claim: A real fundamental divergence (next crop shock) drives a short-lived trend in the spread.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: unscheduled stoppage in those refineries, right? So suddenly suddenly what you have is you have uh that spread will start trending
claims.claim: Refinery outages make crack spreads trend, a transient and diversifying risk factor unrelated to long-term oil.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they use breakout rather than using sort of a smooth trading because you actually are looking for a breakout as an indication of something something fundamental happening there
claims.claim: Use breakout signals on spreads because a break signals a fundamental event.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: But what they're looking for is like the residual volatility, the the difference in movement between the two.
claims.claim: Spread volatility is residual volatility after 90-98% correlation between legs, so it is tiny and needs 50x leverage to matter.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: LTCM bumped up the risk profile by you know 50x 100x and then of course when those spreads we refuse to converge
claims.claim: Leveraging a 2% residual-vol spread is the LTCM trap (on/off the run Treasuries); trade only when the spread becomes volatile.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: becomes 10% of the volatility and now it's interesting it's a it's actually a valid risk factor that you can trade with not too much leverage
claims.claim: After a structural break (tariff, refinery), spread volatility rises from about 2% to about 10% of leg vol, making it tradeable without much leverage.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: a currency basis is the difference between uh funding funding in local currency versus the US
claims.claim: Currency basis moves can trend when transient funding pressure arises (e.g., bond issuance in USD), so they are another transient factor to trade with strict risk rules.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the ability to say I'm going to wait until there is a sufficient risk to start trading it um and then I'm going to get out of this when when there isn't enough volatility
claims.claim: Trade transient factors only while their volatility is sufficient, exit when it fades.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: relative value trades are called relative value because uh it's value rather than trend. So making money out of spreads is more difficult.
claims.claim: Making money from spreads is harder than from outrights because relative value is value-based rather than trend-based.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: maybe the first 25% of of PCA factors trend very well sort of then then we have like a 50% of the remaining uh PCA factors and they do trend
claims.claim: In bond markets the top principal components trend very well and cover about 70% of risk, the middle ones still trend but smaller.
claims.direction: trade top and middle PCA factors

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they tend to actually move in the opposite direction. So they will tend to be uh actually very strongly mean reverting.
claims.claim: The lowest PCA factors (pure RV trades) are strongly mean-reverting, not trending.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: Or maybe you want to upweight the middle factors because although they are they are they they trend less
claims.claim: Remove the smallest factors and overweight middle factors in a PCA-based trend system.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: fast but not as fast as you think
claims.claim: Spread trend should be traded faster than outright trend but not too fast because costs bite.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the notional amount that I trade is higher and therefore my trading cost will be higher. So like per turnover the spread will be more expensive than trading outright.
claims.claim: Spreads cost more per unit of risk since both legs trade, so fast spread trend may be uneconomic.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the back of the curve looks cheap while the front of the curve looks dear. If you if momentum wants to buy something then maybe you should buy the back.
claims.claim: Use curve spreads to choose which contract to trade: if momentum wants to buy and the back is cheap, buy the back (supply/demand driven) rather than the front (macro driven).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: these days everybody is trading copper and as a result the copper has become sort of more speculative in nature right
claims.claim: Copper has become more speculative (CTAs, multistrats) at the front of the curve, seen in volume vs open interest and COT.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they tend to trade more slowly so there's less volume there is more open interest
claims.claim: Hedgers and producers dominate further out the curve, trade slowly, and give open interest with less volume, so contract dynamics differ along the curve.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: But if there's a lot of hedggers in a market, then there and they're risk averse, then in theory there's a there is a premium a risk.
claims.claim: Where many risk-averse hedgers exist, speculators can earn a risk premium.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: some an argument which comes up quite often is to say oh uh trend is at capacity.
claims.claim: Clients argue trend underperformed because too much money is in trend; Man's AUM argument says industry AUM is constant.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: Um the problem with this argument is that there is tons of trend being done at other places where you don't see it.
claims.claim: Industry AUM understates trend capital since QIS and multistrat pods also run trend.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if the industry was overly trend reliant then what you would see is you would see a good correlation yeah a beta between the speculators positioning in the cult report to your signal
claims.claim: Test crowding by regressing speculators' COT positions on trend signals; high beta would signal crowded trend.
claims.indicator: COT speculator positioning vs trend signal

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the speculators have become very sensitive to volatility. So the loading on changes in volatility i.e. if volatility goes up the it goes the speculators uh proportion goes down.
claims.claim: Speculators cut positions when volatility rises, a dominant effect now (volatility-based risk targeting).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: What we don't see is we don't see like suddenly a huge rise or in fact any rise whatsoever in terms of the loading on on slow trend or mid-frequency trend in the data.
claims.claim: Loading on fast trend declined since the early 2000s while CTAs migrated to slow trend; slow trend loading did not rise, so the capacity argument is not supported.
claims.indicator: COT loading on trend by speed

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the amount of daily trading in FX is something like 7.5 trillion
claims.claim: The FX market trades about 7.5 trillion daily (BIS 2022), dwarfing equities and including corporates, asset managers and funds.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: They have 100 million transactions, millions of transactions in the London FX markets from 2015 to 2020. And it's non anonymized.
claims.claim: A Bank of England-led paper (Topography of the FX derivative market) uses regulator-level non-anonymized London FX derivative data for 2015-2020.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: a lot of quans again rush into here's a trading strategy. Sit back just just look at the data. Let it tell you a story.
claims.claim: Describe data structure first before building predictive strategies; avoid overcomplicated models.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: it behooves us as corns rather than just shoving it into a machine to really understand what's going on
claims.claim: Understand the data before using machine learning on it.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: most of it is up to one one week uh expiry right and and that's the most liquid part
claims.claim: FX market makers hold risk in contracts up to one week; hedge funds and asset managers trade 1-3 months (IMM dates); corporates hold 2-3 year swaps, each in their own habitat along the curve.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the hedge funds uh specs their net exposures to the dollar euro and sterling fluctuate a lot
claims.claim: Hedge fund net FX exposures fluctuate widely, while dealers hold the opposite of hedgers.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: there's a structural short dollar for UK corporates right because they have they hedge their dollars back to the UK
claims.claim: UK corporates are structurally long sterling/short dollar from hedging, and dealers hold the opposite; US corporates are the unseen mirror position.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the amount of risk which is available on the market that you are you are able to hold is actually not not not that great
claims.claim: Post-GFC dealers cannot hold large risk on their books, so risk is passed through to corporates and others in bonds, credit and FX.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the top five dealer and the top five market makers really dominate the everything
claims.claim: The FX derivative market is star-shaped: the top five dealers and five market makers dominate, much more than 20 years ago.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the emergence of players like the the non-bank um market makers so like the XTX and the J Street
claims.claim: FX spot is structured differently, with non-bank market makers, while derivatives are concentrated in few counterparties which may be a cause for concern.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Vanguard kind of going against the tide a little bit by suggesting they're suggesting 7030 is the optimal for the next decades
claims.claim: Vanguard recommends a 70/30 style allocation (bond-heavy, 30% equity per Yoav) despite BlackRock's hedge fund call.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: we actually do try to figure out the the beta let's say the equity beta on each of the uh data sets and we fit the the P&L of each of uh the people that we allocate to
claims.claim: An allocator estimates the equity beta of each manager's P&L to track hidden equity exposure.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: we exclude you guys, we exclude CTAs because you guys change, you change your mind too too often
claims.claim: Allocators cannot fit CTA positioning from P&L because CTAs change exposure too often, showing CTAs' lack of persistent correlation.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: that's actually probably one of the most important decisions that you have to make about you know what's the proportion between equities and bonds
claims.claim: The strategic equity-bond split, derived from 10-year capital market assumptions and a correlation matrix, is the allocator's key decision.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: most most of these models are mean reverting by nature i.e. If equities go up, they will actually underweight equity.
claims.claim: Long-horizon CMA-based allocators are mean-reverting: after equities rise they cut expected return and underweight equity, taking the opposite side of trend.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they only cut 50% of it. So we we they cut the expect long-term expectation to to equity by half a percent based on actually very short-term change in equities.
claims.claim: Vanguard cut its 10-year equity return forecast by half the June 2025 rally (10-11%), leading to a 30% equity / 70% bond allocation.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: we kind of don't like them because they they have been negative equity for years
claims.claim: Allocators dislike valuation-based models that have been underweight equity for years.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: equity has been has been uh has been rising quite happily regardless of what Vanguard is saying
claims.claim: Selling equities after the June rally would have done poorly, as the S&P rose from 6.2k to 6.4k.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: all of these very long-term 10-year horizon things um uh all of these are uh maybe make sense if you're investing for 100 years
claims.claim: Long-horizon valuation metrics (Shiller PE, 10-year views) are only useful for very long horizons, not for tactical use.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the role of trend not necessarily as a long-term but as a tactical as a long-term right but as a tactical way of you phasing in that long-term view
claims.claim: Trend can phase in or out a long-term allocation tactically, e.g. delay deallocating from equities while trend is strong.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you will be able to create an optimal allocation over a much wider set of parameters
claims.claim: Including systematic strategies in the optimization automatically adjusts the allocation as assumptions change.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: CTAs will modulate your overall equity exposure. So, if you have 50% equities and you have 20% CTA, you're going to pick up some more equity exposure in your CTA allocation
claims.claim: A CTA allocation adds or removes equity exposure with the equity trend (long in bull, short in bear), a favorable portfolio effect.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: now we got the we're adding strategies such as CTA which are trading some of the assets that you're diversifying
claims.claim: Mean-variance frameworks were designed for assets, not for strategies that trade those same assets, creating a conceptual problem.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: they are playing in a different time horizon than you they're playing at the three-month horizon
claims.claim: Active traders operate at a three-month horizon, invisible to 10-year allocators, which is why they are uncorrelated and long-term allocators should not worry about their positioning.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: in terms of alpha, you just think of it as almost an independent play
claims.claim: Treat CTA/systematic alpha as independent of the CMA allocation, using its positioning only to modulate small tactical changes.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: some systematic strategies like FX hedging are part of the way that you embed are embedded into your process
claims.claim: Allocators already embed systematic strategies such as FX hedging and could embed trend as another tool.
